situation:
You and your partner are the director of human resources and the director of brand marketing for IRONLEAF FITNESS, a chain of forty-one gym and fitness clubs. The founder (judge) opened the first club nineteen years ago, still owns the company, and has signed a letter of intent to sell it this fall. The founder (judge) has asked the two of you to meet this afternoon.

The chain has been profitable for eleven straight years, and much of that growth traces to one contracted head trainer who is the face of the brand. His image carries the chain's current video campaign across social feeds, in-club screens, and email promotions, and four items on the juice bar menu are named for his training programs. That same campaign is licensed to launch with the chain's first clubs overseas.

Last week a front desk employee filed a written harassment complaint against the head trainer. The employee handbook routes complaints to a regional manager who has been on medical leave since June. The trainer denies the allegation and points to a clause in his contract guaranteeing that his image runs through the season. The purchase agreement obligates the founder (judge) to disclose any pending claim before closing.

The founder (judge) could interview both parties personally this week, close the matter quickly, and leave the campaign and the menu items untouched. That path spends nothing and keeps the sale on schedule, but if the complaint is later substantiated the chain will have kept the trainer in front of members after notice, and the buyer can reopen the price over what was disclosed.

Outside counsel could instead run the investigation while the video comes down from every channel and the named menu items are pulled from the juice bar. That approach buys an independent record, but it bills by the hour, pushes the closing past the founder's date, invites members and staff to speculate about a trainer who vanished from the brand, and risks a defamation claim if nothing is substantiated.

The founder (judge) wants the two of you to weigh what the chain owes the employee, the trainer, and its members, and to recommend how this complaint will be investigated and what happens to the campaign and the menu items meanwhile. You will present to the founder (judge) in a meeting in the founder's office. The founder (judge) will greet you and ask to hear your ideas. After you have presented and answered the founder's questions, the founder (judge) will thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the founder (judge) and sole owner of IRONLEAF FITNESS, the gym and fitness club chain you started nineteen years ago and have agreed to sell this fall. Business background is the same as the situation above. You received the harassment complaint against your contracted head trainer last week, and you have not yet decided who will look into it or whether the campaign built on that trainer's image, and the juice bar items named for his programs, stay up while it is looked into.

You want the director of human resources and the director of brand marketing to tell you what the company owes the employee who filed, what it owes the trainer who denies the allegation, and what it owes the members who see him on every screen in every club. You want a recommendation on how the investigation is handled and on what happens to the campaign and the menu items in the meantime.

After the participants have presented and have answered your questions, you will ask the following questions of each participant team:
judgeQuestions: If we had handed this to outside counsel the day it came in, what would that have cost us?
If we leave the campaign up and the complaint holds up, what do we tell our members and our staff?
